source: Tsui (2025) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot in LLMs (full text, v2)
finding: The same injected error is fixed far more often when shown as the user's than as the model's own. Reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot. Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model closes most of the gap.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models; average blind spot 64.5%. Accuracy own-error vs external-error (aggregate): SCLI5 0.499 vs 0.910; GSM8K-SC 0.183 vs 0.881; PRM800K-SC 0.200 vs 0.620. Wait trigger: 0.957 / 0.796 / 0.504 (gain +91.9% / +335.1% / +152.0%); But 0.922 / 0.611 / 0.430; However 0.897 / 0.602 / 0.438. Wait cuts the blind spot 89.3% on average. Macro accuracy base / base+Wait / reasoning sibling: DeepSeek-V3 0.578 / 0.918 / R1 0.908; phi-4 0.325 / 0.704 / reasoning-plus 0.707; Qwen3-32B 0.046 / 0.791 / thinking 0.894. Items: SCLI5 286, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448.
quote: reasoning models are much better at self-correcting their own error
limits: Errors are injected, not natural. Open models only (needs prefix injection), so no o-series or Claude. Fixed 1,024-token budget, temperature 0. Judge is an LLM (gemini-2.5-flash-preview), 100 samples hand-checked per set. Math and recall only. Training-data cause is a hypothesis. Tokens are NOT matched between base+Wait and the base.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: a reasoning model already behaves like base+Wait, so a Wait cue adds little for it. For a non-reasoning agent, a cheap re-evaluation cue (or re-presenting its step as someone else's) is the one self-correction lever with a large measured effect. Open: effect per token versus resampling.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey (TACL)
finding: Survey finds no prior work showing successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Reliable external feedback works. Large-scale fine-tuning works.
numbers: Three findings only, no pooled numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page read, not the full paper. Covers 2023-2024 non-reasoning models. Lists flaws in earlier studies: vague questions, unfair comparison, oracle use.
agent_relevance: Confirms K01/K02 from an independent review. Gate revisions on an external check, not on the model's opinion.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: At equal sample count, sequential revision beats parallel sampling only narrowly. Easy questions favour pure sequential compute. Hard questions favour a mix. Compute-optimal allocation by difficulty matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute. A naive revision model flips many correct answers.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* on MATH. Revision model trained on up to 4 wrong answers in context. About 38% of correct answers were revised into wrong ones by the naive revision model. Mitigated by sequential majority voting or verifier selection over the chain. Starting split about sqrt(N) parallel x sqrt(N) sequential. Exact accuracies only in figures.
limits: One model family, one benchmark, a fine-tuned revision model (not intrinsic prompting). The 38% flip is for the revision model before mitigation. Text gives no exact accuracy numbers (first 100k of 110k characters read).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (partial): revision is competitive with resampling only when selected by vote or verifier and when the question is easy. For hard items add parallel samples. Always keep the original as a candidate.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the dark side of LLMs' intrinsic self-correction (full text)
finding: Intrinsic self-correction turns many correct answers wrong, including on o1 and DeepSeek R1. On a decision-making task o1-mini changes 92.3% of its correct answers to wrong. Repeating the question and a small fine-tune lower the flip rate.
numbers: Yes/No task, correct->wrong rate: o1-preview 13.2%, o1-mini 15.6%, GPT-4o 11.3%, GPT-3.5 34.0%, Llama-3.1-8B 58.8%, Llama-3-8B 58.2%, Llama-2-7B 26.5%, DeepSeek R1 7.9%, DeepSeek V3 28.5%. o1-preview accuracy 78.7% (down 4.9), o1-mini 74.1% (down 4.2). Complex tasks, o1-mini / 4o / 3.5: decision making 92.3 / 76.6 / 76.5%; reasoning 9.1 / 17.9 / 19.7%; programming 14.8 / 21.9 / 28.3%. Mitigation (Yes/No): GPT-4o 11.3% -> 6.0% with question repeating -> 0% with SFT; GPT-3.5 34.0 -> 23.1 -> 0.
limits: Self-correction prompt is a generic review request, not a reasoning-model-native mode. Tokens not matched. The paper's delta labels disagree with its accuracy values in places. The SFT fix was trained on the same yes/no format, so 0% is an in-distribution number. o1 not fine-tuned.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: partial answer. Reasoning-class models are better than 2023 models but still flip 8-16% of correct yes/no answers, and the effect depends strongly on task (decision making is catastrophic). Re-asking 'are you sure?' is not safe even for o1. Repeating the question first is a cheap, measured mitigation.

source: Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: the signal is diagnostic, not causal (2026)
finding: Activation probes on the first reasoning step predict that the final answer will be wrong, much better than verbalised confidence or the text itself. Every attempt to use that signal to fix the answer failed.
numbers: MATH-500, probe trained on 100 problems, tested on 200. Qwen2.5-3B probe AUROC 0.953 (first step only 0.787), verbalised confidence 0.674, self-consistency N=5 0.823, text-only TF-IDF 0.590. Qwen2.5-7B 0.737, 72B 0.977 (CV), DeepSeek-R1-7B 0.852. Steering best +0.03 to +0.04 (3B 0.53->0.56; 7B 0.60->0.64; 3B at alpha 8 -0.06). Probe best-of-12: 0.62 (3B) and 0.70 (7B) vs greedy 0.60 / 0.70, majority vote 0.75 / 0.75, oracle 0.88 / 0.91. Always-retry self-correction: -3 points; oracle-triggered retry: +1 point. Verbalised confidence 4.55/5 on wrong vs 4.87/5 on right traces.
limits: Small open models (1.5B-72B plus one R1 distill), one benchmark; needs white-box access. Baselines differ between tables (3B greedy 0.53 vs 0.60). No Wait-prompt test. Not an API-model result.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 4: error is detectable early with internal access (AUROC 0.95), but that does not give a fix; plain majority vote (0.75) beats the probe-guided pick. For a scaffold with API-only access, sample agreement is the practical gate; a zero-token error locator is not available.

source: Amplified Does Not Mean Predictive: reasoning behaviours in thinking models (2026)
finding: Thinking models self-correct much more often than instruct models, but self-correction is only a modest marker of a right answer. Calibration and knowledge alignment predict correctness far better. Uncertainty talk is amplified 3-7x yet is negatively linked to correctness.
numbers: 15 open models 3B-9B, 6 benchmarks. Behavioural Lift = P(correct | behaviour) - P(correct | absent). Self-correction lift +20.1% (VLM), +12.4% (LLM); present in 21-55% of thinking responses vs 3-15% of instruct. Qwen3-4B MATH-500 within-question accuracy difference +0.27 (thinking) vs +0.08 (instruct). Among traces with a detected failure, self-correction goes with +39 points recovery. On lucky-guess traces self-correction appears 46.2% vs 24.0% on sound traces. Calibration lift +72.2% / +79.6%; uncertainty acknowledgement -16.1% / -13.9%; hypothesis testing +1.0%.
limits: Association, not causation (the model may self-correct because it is on the right track). Labels from a GPT-4o judge. Visible traces only. The prompting experiment is preliminary and GPQA differences not significant.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: in reasoning models, self-correction text is common but does not itself mark quality; do not treat 'I double-checked' as evidence. Use it as a trigger only when paired with a recovery measure.

source: The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (2026)
finding: Spontaneous mid-reasoning shifts ('aha') are rare and usually go with lower accuracy. Artificially forcing a reconsideration helps, most where entropy is high.
numbers: 11M+ traces; shifts in about 6.31% of traces, formal Aha in 1.79%. Qwen2.5-1.5B pooled N=723,200: 2.57% correct with a shift vs 16.44% without. Math: 14.4 vs 32.7%. Qwen2.5-7B Math 28.2 vs 66.1%; Llama-3.1-8B 28.2 vs 45.7%; GPT-4o on MATH-500 33.8 vs 65.8%; DeepSeek-R1 20.4 vs 54.3%. Forced reconsideration on Math: 32.21 -> 40.62% (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wins vs 23,500 losses); Xwords +0.45 pp (5,380 vs 5,004). Spontaneous shifts did not help under high entropy.
limits: Training is GRPO on small models. The shift/no-shift gap is confounded by problem difficulty (hard items have more shifts). Forced reconsideration cost in tokens not compared with resampling in the part read (first 100k of 250k characters).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2: a forced re-look helped (+8.4 pp on Math, wins 2.15x losses) while spontaneous second-guessing signals trouble. Supports gating the re-look on uncertainty, and reading a self-reported shift as a warning sign rather than a repair.

source: The Shape of Overthinking: backtracking bursts in long reasoning traces (2026)
finding: Wrong reasoning traces contain more and later clusters of backtracking. A burst-aware early exit is a cheap trace-level flag, though it is no better than a hard length cutoff at depth.
numbers: Qwen3-8B thinking, AIME24 (3,000 traces, base accuracy 73.2%), AIME25 (3,000 traces, 64.5%), GPQA-Diamond, OmniMath. Mean multi-burst count correct/wrong 1.90 / 4.78 (AIME24, T>=20). Prefix policy retained accuracy AIME24/25: 2k words 73.5/64.5 (drop 21.7/27.0%); 12k words 79.4/69.3 (drop 26.8/35.0%). A plain 12k hard cutoff did better: 80.6/71.7. No AUROC reported.
limits: One main model, 30-problem sets, word counts not tokens, no AUROC. The paper does not show burst features beat a length cutoff.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a free trace-level signal exists (backtrack count) but is weak as a locator. Treat many late backtracks as 'stop and resample', not as 'revise here'.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: identifying process errors in mathematical reasoning (full tables)
finding: Finding the earliest wrong step needs a strong reasoning model. Small trained PRMs and non-reasoning critics both fall off on hard problems, and many also falsely flag correct solutions.
numbers: 3,400 cases. F1 average over GSM8K/MATH/OlympiadBench/Omni-MATH: o1-mini 87.9; QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5; GPT-4o 61.9; Llama-3.3-70B 58.0; Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct 45.5; authors' PRM800K PRM 56.5; Skywork-PRM-7B 42.1; Math-Shepherd 31.5. False-flag rate on correct solutions (100 minus correct accuracy), GSM8K/MATH/Olympiad/Omni: o1-mini 2.1/4.9/4.4/8.3; QwQ 4.7/20.7/45.4/32.0; GPT-4o 8.8/23.4/41.6/34.4; Skywork-PRM-7B 17.1/30.8/68.1/58.1. Missed-error rate (100 minus error accuracy) o1-mini 11.1/16.5/19.8/25.2.
limits: Math only, solutions made by other models. o1-mini used once; open models used 8-vote majority. Tool summary of the tables; one column mapping (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM) is the authors' own trained model.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answered for math: the locator that reaches the 60-70% bar is a reasoning-class model (o1-mini F1 87.9, false flags 2-8%); a 7B PRM is below it and flags 17-68% of correct work on hard sets. Cost is a full reasoning call per solution, not cheap.

source: Decoding the critique mechanism in large reasoning models (2026)
finding: Reasoning models often keep a planted error in their chain but still give the right final answer (hidden correction). A steering vector for critique raises error detection a few points and helps Wait budget forcing.
numbers: Models Qwen3-4B, R1-Distill-8B/14B/32B. On GSM8K-Error, 55-78% of R1 cases end correct with the error left in the trace; explicit corrections under 6%. Qwen3-4B backtracks explicitly in 42.7% (GSM8K-Error) and 81.9% (MATH500-Error). Natural faulty chains: recovery only 0.0-1.9%. Steering: ProcessBench +5%; BIG-Bench Mistake Qwen3-4B 52% -> 56%; Qwen3-4B GSM8K-Error about 77% -> nearly 90% (alpha +1) and just above 50% (alpha -1). Standard benchmarks Table 4, Qwen3-4B GSM8K 57.7 -> 62.9; MATH500 93.0 -> 92.8; AIME gains one problem or fewer.
limits: Open small models, white-box steering, errors are injected single arithmetic mistakes. Positive steering sometimes alters correct steps (not quantified). Wait budget forcing curves only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2: reasoning models already repair injected errors quietly, so the self-correction blind spot is mostly gone for them on easy planted errors. Natural errors are still almost never repaired (under 2%).

source: Disagreement-guided strategy routing: when to vote, when to rewrite (2026)
finding: Use sample disagreement to decide the strategy: accept when two samples agree, vote when a second pair agrees, rewrite the problem only when disagreement is severe. This beats majority vote at a similar sample cap.
numbers: Cap of 6 samplings. Average accuracy over 7 math benchmarks (8K context): Qwen3-8B baseline 61.3, majority 68.9, best-of-N 63.4, proposed 75.8; Qwen3-4B 60.4 / 68.0 / 65.3 / 73.2; DS-Llama-8B 60.4 / 66.2 / 64.3 / 69.4. Qwen3-8B AIME24: majority 50.0, proposed 66.7; Olympiad 50.7 vs 61.9. Uses about 40-60% of the cap on Math500 and 70% on AIME24. Ablation Math500: baseline 84.4, rewrite-only 90.4, vote-only 87.6, full 92.8. Rewriting hurt when a simple question was compressed.
limits: Math only, short contexts, small models. Token cost shown only in a figure. Rewrite can turn a correct answer wrong by dropping conditions.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: sample disagreement is a free gate for revision when no checker exists, and it spends budget only on hard items. Matches the schema idea: revise only when samples disagree.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated errors in large language models (ICML)
finding: Models from different companies share errors well above chance, and the more accurate the models, the more their errors line up. A judge inflates the accuracy of weaker models, most for same-provider ones.
numbers: 350+ LLMs. Mean agreement when both err: HELM 0.60 (chance 1/3), HuggingFace 0.423 (chance about 0.12). 100% of HF pairs and 97.5% of HELM pairs above chance. Top pair agrees on 0.9987 of questions both get wrong. Regression R-squared for agreement 0.340 (HF), 0.613 (HELM), 0.415 (resumes). Same architecture +0.076; same company +0.066 (HF), +0.022 (HELM). Resume task: 20 LLMs, 1,800 pairs.
limits: Multiple-choice leaderboards and resume screening, not agent traces. Judge-inflation figures only in figures (none in text). Same-model generator-to-checker agreement is not measured; it is assumed higher.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a second layer from the same family removes less than independence would. Pick the checker from a different provider or use a non-LLM check; a checker of equal accuracy still shares most errors (agreement 42-60% vs chance 12-33%).

source: Kuai et al. (2026) A statistical framework for auditing behavioural dependence and induced bias in LLM judges
finding: Eighteen LLMs from six families show significant shared failures. Judges with more entanglement with the generator over-endorse wrong answers more. Reweighting by independence improves a verifier ensemble.
numbers: 18 LLMs, 6 families. Over-endorsement vs entanglement index: MMLU-Pro Spearman rho 0.508 (BEI), 0.520 (CIG), p<0.01; MATH-500 rho 0.441, 0.457, p<0.05. De-entangled reweighting vs majority vote: +3.5 points accuracy, +2.6 points precision.
limits: Abstract page only. Index definitions not read. Correlations, not an intervention on a single generator-checker pair.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: shared-failure rate between generator and judge predicts how often the judge approves a wrong answer. Weight cross-family checks higher than same-family ones.

source: Lee et al. (2026) Risk-controlled selective LLM answering by pricing label-free checks (PriceCheck)
finding: Label-free checks such as re-solving can be priced by how often they agree on right and wrong answers, then combined so that served answers meet a target error rate, with abstention on the rest.
numbers: Math held-out selective risk below 1.5% on all 15 splits. Average coverage 76.1% (about 24% abstain). Predicted vs observed coverage rank correlation 0.97 over 118 schedules. Fewest wrong answers at matched coverage vs reward models, prompted judge, generator confidence and a trained classifier.
limits: Abstract page only. Generator and verifier models not named there; benchmarks not named; a small labelled calibration set is needed.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: with no ground truth, a priced stack of re-solve checks plus abstention is the best measured gate. The agent should be allowed to say not-sure rather than force a revision.

source: UPTURN: Inject a turn, not a token (2026)
finding: Where and how a correction is injected matters. A new user turn at a learned position redirects reasoning, while inline reflection tokens did not reliably do so under a fixed budget.
numbers: Four reasoners, six math benchmarks, GPQA-Diamond transfer. A 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder picks the position, trained on final-answer correctness only. Beats a 32-rollout baseline in every setting and self-correction and reflection-token baselines at matched correction budgets; no numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only: no accuracy, no model names, no token cost. No Wait baseline is mentioned.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a cue framed as a separate turn (another speaker) is the form that worked, in line with d01. A tiny trained locator is possible (130K parameters).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing a reasoning model to continue with Wait instead of stopping raises accuracy a little on hard sets, then flattens. Wait beats Hmm and Alternatively.
numbers: s1-32B, 2x extrapolation: AIME24 50.0 -> 53.3 with Wait (50.0 for none, Alternatively, Hmm); MATH500 93.0 for none, Wait and Hmm; GPQA 57.6 -> 59.6. Suppressions on s1: AIME24 50.0, 53.3, 53.3, 56.7 for 0, 1x, 2x, 4x; AIME25 26.7, 30.0, 33.3, 36.7. s1.1: AIME24 56.7 flat; MATH500 94.4 -> 95.4. Flattens at about 6x; too many suppressions cause loops; 12 of 30 AIME24 items overflowed context at 512 steps.
limits: One 32B model fine-tuned on 1,000 examples. AIME has 30 problems: one problem is 3.3 points. Majority-vote comparison is in a figure. Accuracy comes with more tokens; no resample-per-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a Wait cue on a reasoning model helps a little on hard math and not on easy items; the gain is one or two problems. It is not shown to beat resampling per token.

source: McAleese et al. (2024) LLM critics help catch LLM bugs
finding: Trained critics write review comments that people prefer over human reviews, catch more bugs than paid reviewers, but sometimes invent bugs. A human plus critic team hallucinates less than the critic alone.
numbers: Critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases (naturally occurring LLM errors). Hundreds of errors found in training data rated flawless. No hallucination rate on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. Critic is RL-trained on a code task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a critic with a false-bug rate needs a second filter. A human or a test run in the loop lowers invented bugs. Suggests: a critic must give evidence that a check can confirm before any change.

source: Yeung and Summerfield (2012) Metacognition in human decision-making: confidence and error monitoring
finding: Error detection fits an evidence-accumulation account: after a wrong choice, later evidence drifts toward the correct option; after a right choice it keeps reinforcing. Confidence tracks the decision variable at the time of judgement.
numbers: Flanker task error rates can exceed 20% on incompatible trials under speed pressure. In antisaccade tasks people corrected all errors but detected only about half. ERN within about 100 ms; Pe 200-400 ms later tracks conscious detection. Correction can occur within 10-20 ms, so detection and correction are partly separate. Resulaj et al.: more switches from wrong to right than the reverse.
limits: First 100k of 124k characters read. Review text, no direct test of post-commit accumulation beating a fixed monitor. Human perceptual tasks, not reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open for LLMs: no LLM study found that lets an agent keep reading evidence after committing and flags errors by confidence change. d07 (forced reconsideration, entropy-gated) is the nearest.

source: Helmreich (2000) On error management: lessons from aviation (BMJ)
finding: Observed flights show errors are routine and mostly managed. Error should be managed, not eliminated. Violations are a large share of errors, and teams that violate are more likely to commit other errors.
numbers: LOSA: 3,500+ flights; average two threats and two errors per flight. More than half of observed errors were violations. Teams that violated procedures were 1.4 times more likely to commit other error types. About 70% of aviation accidents attributed to human error (NASA). 30% of ICU staff in one US teaching hospital denied committing errors.
limits: The article gives no detection or trapping rate and no slip/lapse/mistake split; per-type consequential rates are only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for rates of slips, lapses, mistakes and recovery. Proficiency and decision errors are rare but more often consequential, so checks belong at decisions, not only at the end.

source: He et al. (2024) Human error in university laboratories using improved CREAM and SPAR-H (Heliyon)
finding: CREAM and SPAR-H were applied to one lab task (14 actions). Their predicted error probabilities differ about six-fold, and neither was checked against observed error counts.
numbers: 23 students, 4 sub-tasks, 14 actions. CREAM mean HEP 0.062 (range 0.003-0.196); SPAR-H mean 0.384 (0.044-0.867). Heinrich-ratio estimate of about 0.02 unsafe behaviours per operation (21 injuries, about 217 unsafe behaviours, about 11,592 operations). By education CREAM: PhD 0.0366, postgraduate 0.0466, undergraduate 0.113. CPC weight set to 1 gives 0.008.
limits: No validation against observed error rates; weights from 8 experts; one lab; data not public. The 0.02 comparison point is an industrial ratio, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a CREAM HEP differs by a factor of six from another method on the same task; no evidence that CREAM predicts measured error rates.

source: Shirali et al. (2019) Modifying a method for human reliability assessment based on CREAM-BN (petrochemical control room)
finding: A Bayesian-network version of CREAM was built from a 70-item questionnaire and agrees roughly with basic CREAM. It was not compared with observed error data.
numbers: 60 respondents returned (62 asked), four positions. Content validity ratio 0.72; Cronbach alpha 0.78. Basic CREAM HEP 0.01 / 0.01 / 0.02 / 0.01 vs BN HEP 0.03 / 0.03 / 0.08 / 0.09 for head of control, shift supervisor, boardman, outside operator. Reviewer recalculation does not match two reported values.
limits: Validation is agreement with CREAM itself only. Self-designed questionnaire. Inconsistent reporting. Single unit.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: still no quantitative validation of CREAM predictions. Use CREAM only as a vocabulary for classifying agent failures (observation, interpretation, planning, execution), not as a rate predictor.

source: Roll et al. (2019) Human error: job insecurity, attention-related cognitive errors and error detection
finding: In a paper check task (match fictitious orders to receipts) people missed about half the planted errors, and false alarms were rare.
numbers: N=148 employees (Shanghai). 12 test trials, 10 planted errors, 1 min 45 s per trial. Mean misses 54.28% (SD 22.05), so about 46% detected; false positives 1.84% (SD 3.01). Self-reported attention errors correlate with misses r=0.19; burnout with misses r=0.16.
limits: Cross-sectional, self-report predictors, one task; the page text has an internal statistical inconsistency. First 100k of 125k characters read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a human fixed-time review catches under half of planted errors but raises almost no false alarms, the reverse of the LLM critic profile (many false flags). Supports pairing a low-false-alarm check with the LLM.

source: Hollnagel CREAM as summarised in a 2023 radiogram HRA paper (arXiv 2310.14697); intervals via secondary sources
finding: CREAM has four control modes (scrambled, opportunistic, tactical, strategic) chosen from nine common performance conditions, with 13 generic failure types; error probability falls from scrambled to strategic. The paper's interval and failure-type tables are images, so the numbers were not read there.
numbers: Intervals as quoted by search summaries of secondary papers (not read in the book): strategic 0.5E-5 to 1E-2; tactical 1E-3 to 1E-1; opportunistic 1E-2 to 0.5; scrambled 0.1 to 1.0. The paper says COCOM was validated by independent studies (Stanton 2001); not checked.
limits: Hollnagel 1998 book not opened. Intervals overlap, so a mode gives only a coarse band. Treat the numbers as reported by secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Use the idea (context sets control mode); do not cite the numbers as read from the source.

source: Replication of Reason's (1979) diary study of action slips in healthy volunteers
finding: 189 healthy volunteers kept a one-week diary of action slips. Slips were not linked to perceived stress and only weakly to a memory-failures questionnaire.
numbers: N=189; mean 6.4 slips per person per week (SD 4.9). The page does not give Reason's own 1979 counts; the recalled 433 slips and 35 people stay unverified.
limits: Self-report diaries miss slips never noticed; no category percentages on the page.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for Reason's own figures. Slips are frequent and self-noticed, which fits cheap code-level checks.

source: Tsui (2025) Self-Correction Bench v2, Table 3: base vs base+Wait vs reasoning model
finding: Reasoning models show a small or even negative blind spot. Appending Wait to non-reasoning base models recovers most of the gap to their reasoning versions. The paper tests no Claude and no o1; closed models were excluded because prefix injection was needed.
numbers: Macro-average accuracy base / base+Wait / reasoning: DeepSeek-V3 to R1-0528 0.578 / 0.918 / 0.908; phi-4 to reasoning-plus 0.325 / 0.704 / 0.707; Qwen3-14B 0.121 / 0.884 / 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.046 / 0.791 / 0.894; Qwen3-30B-A3B 0.102 / 0.869 / 0.845; Qwen3-235B 0.335 / 0.865 / 0.876. Per-model blind-spot values are only in images.
limits: Open models only. Column order inferred by the reader tool from a garbled header. The earlier Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5% and Sonnet 4 41.4% figures were not found in this version.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: owner-framing matters less for reasoning-trained models. Claude-class not measured.

source: Panickssery, Bowman and Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: Abstract only: GPT-4 and Llama 2 tell their own outputs from others' out of the box; fine-tuning shows a linear link between self-recognition and self-preference bias; controlled tests resist simple confounders.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page; the PDF text could not be read in this session.
limits: Older models, summarisation. No Claude, no reasoning model, no false-pass rate for known-wrong drafts.
agent_relevance: Supports a fresh, different reviewer; gap 2 (Claude false-pass rate) stays open.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Longer reasoning can lower accuracy. Tested Claude Sonnet 3.7, Sonnet 4, Opus 4, o3-mini, o4-mini, o3, Qwen3-32B, QwQ-32B and DeepSeek R1. Claude models get more distracted by irrelevant content; o3 resists distractors but overfits to familiar framings.
numbers: Misleading Math: Opus 4 from near 100% to about 85-90%. Misleading Python: Opus 4 near-perfect to about 80%. R1 with five distractors about 70% to 30%. Zero-shot grade regression: Sonnet 3.7, Opus 4, o3-mini decline; few-shot largely fixes it. Survival-instinct: Sonnet 4 willingness to be turned off 60% to 47%.
limits: First 100k characters read. Synthetic task families. Not about error recovery directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: more thinking is not monotone for Claude models; cap forced reconsideration and keep a best-so-far answer.

source: Tyen et al. (2023) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (backtracking, Table 6)
finding: With the true error location, backtracking helps wrong traces a lot and hurts correct ones a little; with a random location it hurts more. A trained locator breaks even at roughly 60-70% accuracy.
numbers: Delta correct / delta incorrect (points), oracle location: word sorting -11.11/+23.53; tracking shuffled objects -6.67/+43.92; logical deduction -11.43/+36.86; multistep arithmetic 0.00/+18.04; Dyck -6.82/+18.06. Random location: -15.56/+11.76; -6.67/+20.39; -13.33/+21.57; -8.89/+10.59; -15.91/+5.16. Losses plateau near 65% classifier accuracy. 2,186 trace sets, only 45 correct traces per task.
limits: Break-even read from a figure described in the text. BIG-Bench Mistake only; PaLM 2 era; no keep-best-so-far rule tested. The out-of-domain locator did not reach the threshold.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed: about 65% precision needed on this data. Keep-best rule untested; measure on our tasks.

source: Zeng et al. (2023) MR-GSM8K meta-reasoning benchmark
finding: Models are much worse at finding the first wrong step and the reason than at final answers. The paper gives no split into calculation errors versus logic errors.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo zero-shot: TPR 69.5, TNR 91.8; first-error-step accuracy 48.8; error-reason accuracy 46.3; MR-Score 50.5. Of 1,573 wrong solutions the first error step was right for GPT-4 823, Claude2 331, GPT-3.5 179. Qualitative failure types only: reversal curse, unit inconsistency, insensitivity to numerical errors.
limits: Math word problems; no slip or mistake counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Our harness should tag error type itself.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Weaver: shrinking the generation-verification gap with weak verifiers
finding: Combining many weak verifiers (33 reward models and LM judges) beats the best single one and majority vote, but gains shrink with each verifier because of correlated biases on hard examples. Weaver assumes conditional independence to fit weights.
numbers: Average accuracy 87.7% vs 72.7% best single reward model, 72.2% majority vote, 69.1% naive top-10 ensemble (100 generations, Llama 3.3 70B). Up to 15 verifiers: up to +8.5% over top verifier. With about 1% labels accuracy falls 20.1% on average. Correlation itself not measured.
limits: Open verifiers and Llama generators; MATH500, GPQA, MMLU. Not same-family joint miss rates. Last 94k chars unread.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly informed: more reviewers help with diminishing returns and need label-calibrated weights. Same-family joint miss rate unmeasured.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample right) keeps rising with samples, but majority vote and a reward model plateau near 100 samples, so choosing the right sample is the bottleneck without a real verifier.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; best selection 40.50% to 41.41%. SWE-bench Lite: 11.3% of problems have flaky test suites. CodeContests: 35 of 122 reference solutions fail their own tests.
limits: 128-problem subsets; reward model ArmoRM-8B.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 10: when samples share a wrong belief, vote plateaus; executable checks beat judging, but checks themselves can be wrong.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: At equal sample budget self-repair gains are modest, vary by subset and sometimes vanish. Feedback quality is the bottleneck: stronger or human feedback helps much more.
numbers: APPS, GPT-4: 1.05x pass@20 at 10 initial + 1 repair each, 0.97x at 2 initial + 10 repairs. Repair success 33.3% with GPT-4 feedback vs 52.6% with human feedback (1.58x): introductory 42.64 to 62.21, interview 19.33 to 45.67, competition 3.67 to 14.67. HumanEval Code Llama up to about 10% above baseline.
limits: First 100k chars read. 2023 models; feedback is prose, not a code-located line from a test.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: no evidence a code-located error line beats resampling at equal tokens; spend budget on initial samples and strong external feedback.

source: Cook et al. (2024) TICK: generated checklists improve LLM evaluation and generation
finding: Instance-specific checklists, generated and answered item by item by the model, improve agreement with humans and beat plain Self-Refine.
numbers: Exact agreement with humans 46.4% (direct score) vs 52.2% (TICK), GPT-4o judge. STICK: InFoBench +6.5 abs, WildBench +7.1 abs (Command-R+); LiveBench Command-R+ 32.0 to 35.8 while Self-Refine gave 23.7; GPT-4o 55.4 to 56.2 vs Self-Refine 47.1. Best-of-8 InFoBench 0.843 greedy to 0.894.
limits: Checklists are made per item by an LLM, not a fixed code-run list. Body text and abstract disagree on one gain (+5.3 vs +6.3). Last 23k chars unread.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 only indirect: item-by-item checking beats holistic self-scoring; a fixed code-run checklist is untested.

source: Kuhn, Gal and Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty
finding: Entropy over answer meanings flags likely errors better than raw token entropy. It does not test samples that agree on the same wrong answer; its framing implies it would miss them.
numbers: OPT-30B TriviaQA AUROC 0.828 vs 0.802 length-normalised entropy; CoQA 0.7672 vs 0.7533. Cluster count alone 0.79 / 0.66. Entailment classifier 92.7% / 95.3% accurate, 61% at temperature 1.5.
limits: OPT up to 30B, QA only; at stricter ROUGE thresholds normalised entropy wins.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: agreement signals detect uncertainty, not shared-belief errors; add an external check.

source: Viswanathan et al. (2025) Checklists are better than reward models (RLCF)
finding: Checklist-based reward (items answered by a judge, some by small programs) beat reward-model baselines for instruction following. This is training, not a scaffold.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: FollowBench hard satisfaction 71.4 to 75.3; InFoBench 78.1 to 84.1; Arena-Hard 51.3 to 54.6. FollowBench baselines: Skywork 69.5, ArmoRM 70.4, AI judge 70.3. Programs helped slightly on instruct (75.3 vs 73.8), not on base models.
limits: Needs weights; some table rows looked inconsistent; text and table disagree on one relative gain.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: indirect support for checklists over holistic scoring; program verification gain small and mixed.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Execution results (unit tests) as feedback give larger gains than model-only explanation; most gain comes in the first one to three turns.
numbers: TransCoder Codex 80.4 baseline, simple 89.3, unit test 91.6, UT+explanation 92.5; GPT-4 77.3 to 90.4. MBPP GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6. Spider with explanation only +2-3%; Spider greedy plus debug matches 16 samples, and 8 samples plus debug beats 32.
limits: 2023 models; tests were available; last 35k chars unread; token cost not controlled.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: execution-grounded feedback beats extra sampling by sample count on code. Cap rounds at about 3.

source: Wait and think more: overthinking in distilled reasoning models (arXiv 2506.04210)
finding: Repeated Wait helps at first, then accuracy falls. Splitting the same budget into parallel traces with majority vote does better.
numbers: GSM8K, R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: 82.2% to 87.3% when tokens rise from 385 to 1,100, then 70.3% at 15,980. MATH-500: 83.2%, about +1.5 from 2,657 to 4,983 tokens, 78.3% at 16,109. At 16k budget parallel is about 22% above Wait. Entropy 0.23 to 2.79 on GSM8K.
limits: Small distilled models; unreviewed preprint; not Claude.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 mostly closed for small open models: use one or two forced rounds, prefer parallel samples.
